What are the power waves a and b at a port, and why use them instead of V and I?
column2: \(a = (\mathbf V + Z_0\mathbf I)/(2\sqrt{Z_0})\), \(b = (\mathbf V - Z_0\mathbf I)/(2\sqrt{Z_0})\), so the net power is \(\tfrac12(|a|^2 - |b|^2)\). At microwave frequencies opens and shorts are hard to make, but matched loads are easy, and waves are what a VNA measures.

column1: Define \(S_{ij}\) and say what \(|S_{11}|\) and \(|S_{21}|\) mean in dB.
column2: \(S_{ij} = b_i/a_j\) with every other port terminated in \(Z_0\). Return loss is \(-20\log_{10}|S_{11}|\); insertion loss is \(-20\log_{10}|S_{21}|\).

column1: What do reciprocity and losslessness imply for an S-matrix?
column2: Reciprocal (passive, isotropic, no transistors or ferrites): \(S = S^T\). Lossless: \(S^HS = I\), so each column has unit norm. A measured network with \(|S_{11}|^2 + |S_{21}|^2 < 1\) is absorbing power.

column1: Why cascade two-ports with ABCD or T matrices rather than S-matrices?
column2: ABCD and T matrices relate one port's quantities to the other's, so a cascade is a matrix product. S-matrices relate incident to reflected waves and do not multiply; convert, multiply, convert back.

column1: Give \(\Gamma_{in}\) of a two-port terminated in \(\Gamma_L\). When is it equal to \(S_{11}\)?
column2: \(\Gamma_{in} = S_{11} + S_{12}S_{21}\Gamma_L/(1 - S_{22}\Gamma_L)\). It equals \(S_{11}\) when the device is unilateral (\(S_{12} = 0\)) or the load is matched.

column1: State the K–Δ and μ tests for unconditional stability.
column2: \(K = (1 - |S_{11}|^2 - |S_{22}|^2 + |\Delta|^2)/(2|S_{12}S_{21}|) > 1\) with \(|\Delta| < 1\), \(\Delta = S_{11}S_{22} - S_{12}S_{21}\); or the single test \(\mu > 1\), where μ is the distance from the Smith chart's centre to the nearest unstable load.

column1: What are MSG and \(G_{max}\)?
column2: MSG \(= |S_{21}/S_{12}|\), the most gain from a conditionally stable device after resistive loading to K = 1. When K > 1, a simultaneous conjugate match gives \(G_{max} = |S_{21}/S_{12}|(K - \sqrt{K^2 - 1})\), always below MSG.

column1: What does VNA calibration (SOL, TRL) remove?
column2: The systematic errors of the cables and test set: directivity \(e_{00}\), source match \(e_{11}\) and tracking \(e_{10}e_{01}\) in the one-port model \(\Gamma_m = e_{00} + e_{10}e_{01}\Gamma/(1 - e_{11}\Gamma)\). De-embedding then removes fixtures by matrix inversion.

column1: What is the Q of an L-network, and what sets it?
column2: \(Q = \sqrt{R_{high}/R_{low} - 1}\): fixed by the resistance ratio alone, with \(|X| = QR_{low}\) and \(|B| = Q/R_{high}\). A 10:1 ratio needs Q = 3.

column1: How wide is an L-network match?
column2: About \(\Delta f/f_0 \approx 2\Gamma_m/Q\) to reflection \(\Gamma_m\) (more precisely \(2\Gamma_m\sqrt{1 + Q^2}/Q^2\)). Large transformation ratios are narrowband.

column1: Why use π or T networks, or several L-sections?
column2: A π or T network sets Q above the L-network's (narrower, more harmonic filtering); several L-sections through intermediate resistances \(R_{low}(R_{high}/R_{low})^{k/n}\) lower the Q per section and widen the band.

column1: How much does finite component Q cost in a match?
column2: \(\text{IL} \approx 10\log_{10}(1 + Q_n/Q_u)\) dB: the ratio of network Q to component Q. A Q = 3 match with an on-chip inductor of \(Q_u\) = 8 loses about 1.4 dB.

column1: State the Bode–Fano limit for a parallel RC load.
column2: \(\int_0^\infty\ln(1/|\Gamma|)\,d\omega \le \pi/(RC)\); for a flat band, \(\Delta f \le 1/[2RC\ln(1/\Gamma_m)]\). No lossless network of any order beats it: bandwidth and match trade against the load's own Q.

column1: How does a multi-section quarter-wave transformer work?
column2: Small steps make small reflections, \(\Gamma_n \approx \tfrac12\ln(Z_{n+1}/Z_n)\), that add with phase \(e^{-2jn\theta}\). Choosing them binomially gives a maximally flat response; Chebyshev weights give equal ripple and a wider band.

column1: Absorb or resonate: how do you match a complex load?
column2: Either absorb its reactance into the matching network's element (if the sign and size fit) or resonate it out first with an opposite reactance, then match the remaining resistance.

column1: Define noise factor, noise figure and noise temperature.
column2: \(F = (S_i/N_i)/(S_o/N_o)\) with the source at \(T_0\) = 290 K; NF = \(10\log_{10}F\); \(T_e = T_0(F - 1)\). A passive loss L at \(T_0\) has F = L.

column1: State Friis's formula and its lesson.
column2: \(F = F_1 + (F_2 - 1)/G_1 + (F_3 - 1)/(G_1G_2) + \cdots\) with available gains. The first stage dominates once its gain is large; loss before the LNA adds to the noise figure dB for dB.

column1: What are noise parameters?
column2: \(F = F_{min} + (R_n/G_s)|Y_s - Y_{opt}|^2\): the minimum noise factor, the noise resistance (sensitivity to mismatch) and the optimum source admittance. Noise match and power match are generally different.

column1: How does a Y-factor measurement work?
column2: Switch a noise source between hot (\(T_h\)) and cold (\(T_0\)) and measure the output-power ratio Y: \(F = \text{ENR}/(Y - 1)\), equivalently \(Y = 1 + \text{ENR}/F\).

column1: Relate P1dB and IIP3 for a cubic nonlinearity.
column2: \(A_{1dB}^2 = 0.145|a_1/a_3|\) and \(A_{IIP3}^2 = \tfrac43|a_1/a_3|\), so IIP3 − P1dB ≈ 9.64 dB. IM3 rises 3 dB per dB of input, so IIP3 = \(P_{in} + (P_{fund} - P_{IM3})/2\).

column1: How do intercept points cascade?
column2: \(1/\text{IIP3} = 1/\text{IIP3}_1 + G_1/\text{IIP3}_2 + G_1G_2/\text{IIP3}_3 + \cdots\) in linear units: gain before a stage makes its nonlinearity count more. Late stages dominate linearity, early stages noise.

column1: What is reciprocal mixing?
column2: The LO's phase noise mixes a strong blocker onto the wanted channel: \(N_{rm} = P_B + \mathcal L(\Delta f) + 10\log_{10}B\). Blockers set phase-noise specifications.

column1: Write the sensitivity and SFDR of a receiver.
column2: \(P_{sens} = -174 + 10\log_{10}B + \text{NF} + \text{SNR}_{min}\) dBm; \(\text{SFDR} = \tfrac23(\text{IIP3} - N)\), with N the input-referred noise floor.

column1: Why can a resistively terminated LNA not have a noise figure below 3 dB?
column2: A matching resistor equal to the source resistance generates as much noise as the source, so F = 1 + R_s/R_T = 2 (3.01 dB) before any gain.

column1: What noise figure does a matched common-gate LNA reach?
column2: With \(g_m = 1/R_s\), \(F = 1 + \gamma/\alpha\): 2.2 dB for γ/α = 2/3, 3 dB for γ/α = 1, independent of frequency but bounded below.

column1: How does inductive source degeneration create a noiseless 50 Ω?
column2: \(Z_{in} = sL_s + 1/(sC_{gs}) + \omega_TL_s\): the real part \(\omega_TL_s\) comes from feedback, not a resistor. Set \(\omega_TL_s = R_s\) and resonate \(L_g + L_s\) with \(C_{gs}\).

column1: Give the gain and noise figure of the inductively degenerated LNA.
column2: \(Q_{in} = 1/(2\omega_0R_sC_{gs})\), \(G_m = \omega_T/(2\omega_0R_s)\), \(F = 1 + (\gamma/\alpha)g_mR_s(\omega_0/\omega_T)^2\) (drain noise only). A device fast compared with the carrier gives a low NF.

column1: What usually limits a real inductively degenerated LNA's noise figure?
column2: The gate inductor's loss \(r_g = \omega_0L_g/Q_L\), which sits in series with the source: \(F = 1 + r_g/R_s + \ldots\). A few ohms add tenths of a dB, so \(L_g\) is often off-chip or a bond wire.

column1: What does the input network's voltage gain cost?
column2: Linearity: the gate sees \(Q_{in}\) times the source EMF, so the source-referred IIP3 is \(20\log_{10}Q_{in}\) dB below the device's own.

column1: How does a noise-cancelling LNA work?
column2: A common-gate stage matches the input; a common-source stage senses the same node. The matching device's noise appears with opposite signs at the two outputs and cancels when \(g_{m2}R_2 = g_{m1}R_1\), while the signal adds. Wideband match, NF below the CG limit.

column1: What is the conversion gain of an ideal switching mixer?
column2: A square-wave LO's fundamental is \(4/\pi\); the difference term carries half of it, so \(G_c = 2/\pi\) (−3.92 dB) for a passive mixer and \((2/\pi)g_mR_L\) for a Gilbert cell.

column1: Why is an ideal switching mixer's SSB noise figure 3.92 dB?
column2: The signal sits in one sideband but noise from both the signal and image sidebands (and LO harmonics) folds to the IF; for the ideal mixer the SSB noise factor is \(1/G_c^2 = \pi^2/4\).

column1: What sets the image rejection of an I/Q image-reject receiver?
column2: Gain error ε and phase error θ: \(\text{IRR} \approx 4/(\varepsilon^2 + \theta^2)\). About 1% and 1° give roughly 40 dB; calibration is needed beyond that.

column1: How does a harmonic-reject mixer cancel the 3rd and 5th LO harmonics?
column2: Three square-wave LOs at −45°, 0 and +45°, weighted 1, √2, 1, approximate a sampled sine: the nth harmonic is ∝ \(\tfrac1n[\sqrt2 + 2\cos(n\cdot45°)]\), zero for n = 3 and 5. The 7th and 9th remain.

column1: What is an N-path filter?
column2: N switched capacitors driven by non-overlapping LO phases: a high-Q bandpass centred on the LO, with \(\text{BW}_{3dB} = 1/(\pi NR_sC)\) and centre gain \([(N/\pi)\sin(\pi/N)]^2\), tunable with the clock.

column1: Where do LO leakage and second-order distortion hurt most?
column2: In zero-IF receivers: LO leakage self-mixes to a DC offset, and IM2 from a strong blocker lands at DC on top of the wanted signal. Mixer balance (IIP2) and DC-offset cancellation address them.

column1: Active versus passive mixers: the trade?
column2: Active (Gilbert) mixers give gain and isolation but add flicker noise and use headroom; passive mixers are very linear and add no switch flicker noise, but have loss and no reverse isolation: they are transparent to the baseband impedance.

column1: How do the inductor and capacitor Qs combine in an LC tank?
column2: \(1/Q = 1/Q_L + 1/Q_C\), with \(R_p = Q\omega_0L\). On-chip inductors usually dominate, though at millimetre wave the varactors' Q can.

column1: What sets the amplitude of a cross-coupled LC oscillator?
column2: In the current-limited regime the pair switches the tail current: \(V = (2/\pi)I_{tail}R_p\), until the supply limits it (voltage-limited). Start-up needs \(G(V) > 1/R_p\).

column1: Give Leeson's phase noise in the \(1/f^2\) region.
column2: \(\mathcal L(\Delta f) = (2FkT/P_s)[\omega_0/(2Q\Delta\omega)]^2\): higher Q and higher tank power lower it, 6 dB per doubling of Q, 3 dB per doubling of power.

column1: What does the impulse sensitivity function explain?
column2: How noise injected at each phase of the oscillation turns into phase: \(\Gamma(\theta)\). Its rms sets the \(1/f^2\) noise, and its DC value \(\Gamma_{dc}\) converts flicker noise up, giving a \(1/f^3\) corner at \(\omega_{1/f}\Gamma_{dc}^2/\Gamma_{rms}^2\).

column1: Define the oscillator figure of merit.
column2: \(\text{FoM} = -\mathcal L(\Delta f) + 20\log_{10}(f_0/\Delta f) - 10\log_{10}(P_{DC}/1\ \text{mW})\), in dB; good LC VCOs reach the mid-180s to mid-190s.

column1: How does frequency division change phase noise?
column2: An ideal divide-by-N lowers it by \(20\log_{10}N\): 6 dB per halving, because phase deviations are divided by N.

column1: What is injection locking and pulling?
column2: An injected signal near \(\omega_0\) locks the oscillator if within \(\omega_L \approx (\omega_0/2Q)(I_{inj}/I_{osc})\) (Adler); just outside, it pulls and beats. A PA coupling into its own VCO pulls it, which is why transmitters offset the VCO frequency.

column1: How does integrated phase noise set EVM?
column2: \(\phi_{rms}^2 = 2\int\mathcal L(f)\,df\) and EVM ≈ \(\phi_{rms}\); for a PLL flat at \(\mathcal L_0\) to its bandwidth \(f_c\), \(\phi_{rms} \approx \sqrt{\pi\mathcal L_0f_c}\).

column1: What sets a PA's optimum load?
column2: Full voltage swing at the required power: \(R_{opt} = (V_{DD} - V_k)^2/(2P_{out})\). A watt from 3.4 V needs only a few ohms, so the PA needs a large impedance transformation to 50 Ω.

column1: Give the ideal efficiencies of classes A, B and C.
column2: Class A 50%, class B π/4 = 78.5%, class C approaches 100% as the conduction angle α → 0: \(\eta(\alpha) = (\alpha - \sin\alpha)/\{2[2\sin(\alpha/2) - \alpha\cos(\alpha/2)]\}\), with output power falling.

column1: How do classes E and F reach high efficiency?
column2: By shaping waveforms so voltage and current never overlap: class F adds harmonic terminations (88.4% with the 3rd harmonic), class E uses a tuned load for zero-voltage switching (\(P_{out} = 0.577V_{DD}^2/R\)).

column1: Why does PAPR hurt PA efficiency?
column2: The PA must handle the peaks but spends most time well below them, where class A or B efficiency is low: ideal class B averages 29.2% on a 9.64 dB-PAPR OFDM signal against 78.5% at peak.

column1: How does ACLR relate to IIP3?
column2: For a cubic nonlinearity and a Gaussian signal, ACLR (dBc) \(= 2(P_{in} - \text{IIP3}) - 4.77\): 2 dB better per dB of back-off.

column1: How does a Doherty PA keep efficiency in back-off?
column2: A main amplifier sees a raised load (through a quarter-wave inverter) while an auxiliary is off, so it saturates at 6 dB back-off; the auxiliary then lowers the main's load. Ideal efficiency peaks at both 0 and 6.02 dB back-off (78.5%).

column1: What are envelope tracking and DPD?
column2: ET modulates the supply with the envelope so the PA stays near saturation (\(\eta = \eta_{PA}\eta_{mod}\)); DPD applies the inverse nonlinearity in baseband (\(b_3 = -a_3/a_1\) for a cubic) using an observation receiver. Neither can exceed the PA's saturated power.

column1: Where is the image in a superheterodyne?
column2: \(f_{im} = f_{RF} \pm 2f_{IF}\), on the far side of the LO; a high IF eases image filtering but makes channel filtering harder.

column1: What is the half-IF spur?
column2: An input halfway between the RF and the LO: its second harmonic mixes with the LO's second harmonic to the IF. Only f_IF/2 from the wanted signal, it is hard to filter, so it relies on the mixer's second-order linearity.

column1: Why are zero-IF receivers dominant, and what are their problems?
column2: No image (the signal is its own image) and channel filtering at baseband on chip. Problems: DC offsets from LO self-mixing, IM2, flicker noise and I/Q mismatch.

column1: Why does a low-IF receiver need high image rejection?
column2: Its image is an adjacent channel that may be much stronger: \(\text{IRR} \ge (P_{adj} - P_{wanted}) + \text{SNR}_{req}\).

column1: What limits direct RF sampling?
column2: Jitter (\(\text{SNR} = -20\log_{10}(2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t)\)) and the ADC's noise figure, \(\text{NF}_{ADC} = \text{NSD} + P_{FS} + 174\), often over 20 dB, which demands gain ahead of the ADC.

column1: How is a Butterworth preselector's rejection estimated?
column2: \(10\log_{10}(1 + x^{2n})\) with \(x = (f_0/B)(f/f_0 - f_0/f)\): about 20n dB per decade of normalized offset.

column1: What is a complex (polyphase) filter used for?
column2: A filter whose response is asymmetric in frequency, \(H = \omega_p/[\omega_p + j(\omega - \omega_{IF})]\): it passes positive IF frequencies and rejects the image at negative ones in a low-IF receiver.

column1: Describe the Butterworth-Van Dyke model.
column2: A static capacitance \(C_0\) in parallel with a motional \(R_mL_mC_m\) branch. Series resonance \(f_s\); parallel resonance \(f_p = f_s\sqrt{1 + C_m/C_0}\).

column1: What does \(k^2_{eff}\) set?
column2: The spacing of the resonances, \(k^2_{eff} \approx (\pi^2/4)(f_p - f_s)/f_p\), and so the achievable filter bandwidth; Q sets the insertion loss and skirt steepness.

column1: SAW versus BAW: where does each win?
column2: SAW is almost exclusive up to about 1 GHz; above that SAW and BAW compete. SAW electrodes must be patterned at a quarter wavelength, which becomes fine and lossy at high frequency, while BAW resonance is set by a film thickness and scales to 6 GHz and beyond.

column1: Why does TCF matter for duplexers?
column2: An edge drifts by \(f\cdot\text{TCF}\cdot\Delta T\); in a band with a narrow duplex gap, plain SAW at −40 ppm/°C can spend half the gap on drift, so narrow gaps need TC-SAW, IHP-SAW or BAW.

column1: What is an RF switch's figure of merit?
column2: \(R_{on}C_{off}\) in femtoseconds (about 100–120 fs for SOI processes), set by technology. On loss \(20\log_{10}(1 + R_{on}/2Z_0)\); off isolation falls 6 dB/octave as \(C_{off}\) passes signal.

column1: Why are switches stacked?
column2: A PA's swing (14 V peak at 33 dBm in 50 Ω, more under mismatch) exceeds what one thin-film SOI transistor withstands; N in series share the voltage, multiplying \(R_{on}\) by N and dividing \(C_{off}\) by N.

column1: What does an antenna tuner recover?
column2: Mismatch loss \(-10\log_{10}(1 - |\Gamma|^2)\): 1.25 dB at VSWR 3 and 3.1 dB at VSWR 6 when a hand detunes the antenna.

column1: What sets a microstrip patch's size?
column2: Its length is about half a guided wavelength, \(L \approx c/(2f_0\sqrt{\varepsilon_{eff}}) - 2\Delta L\), with fringing extension ΔL; the width sets radiation resistance and bandwidth.

column1: State the Chu–McLean limit.
column2: A small antenna in a sphere of radius a has radiation \(Q \ge 1/(ka)^3 + 1/(ka)\), so bandwidth \(\approx (s - 1)/(Q\sqrt s)\) shrinks as the cube of size; loss widens the band only by wasting power (\(Q_{tot} = \eta Q_{rad}\)).

column1: How does EIRP scale with the number of array elements?
column2: \(N^2\): N times the transmit power and N times the gain, \(\text{EIRP} = N^2P_eG_e\). On receive, SNR and G/T scale as N.

column1: What causes beam squint, and how big is it?
column2: Phase shifters set the right phase only at \(f_0\): \(\sin\theta_{beam} = (f_0/f)\sin\theta_0\). The 3 dB bandwidth toward \(\theta_0\) is about \(0.886f_0/[N(d/\lambda)\sin\theta_0]\); true-time delay removes it.

column1: What does b-bit phase quantization cost?
column2: Gain loss \(S = (\sin x/x)^2\), \(x = \pi/2^b\), and a scattered-power floor \((1 - S)/N\) below the peak (if errors are decorrelated); rms error \(180°/(2^b\sqrt3)\), about 6 dB lower floor per bit.

column1: What is the DC-optimal element count of a transmit array?
column2: \(N^* = \sqrt{E/(G_e\eta P_{oh})}\), where the PA and overhead power are equal; the minimum is flat (25% more power at 2N* or N*/2).

column1: How do grating lobes and scan loss limit an array?
column2: Spacing must satisfy \(d \le \lambda/(1 + |\sin\theta_{max}|)\) at the highest frequency; element gain falls about as cos θ (1.5 dB at 45°, 3 dB at 60°), so arrays scan ±45–60° and phones use several modules.

column1: What is a MIMO radar's virtual array?
column2: Each transmit–receive pair acts as one element at the sum of their positions: \(N_{TX}N_{RX}\) virtual elements from \(N_{TX} + N_{RX}\) antennas, with resolution about \(2/(N_{TX}N_{RX})\) rad.

column1: Write the link-budget ledger and the MAPL.
column2: \(P_r = P_t - L_t + G_t - PL - L_{ex} + G_r - L_r \ge S + M\); MAPL = EIRP + G_r − L_r − S − M − L_ex. Each line has an owner and a cost.

column1: How much range does one decibel buy?
column2: A factor \(10^{1/(10n)}\): 12% per dB in free space (n = 2), 7% at n = 3.5. Every dB anywhere in the ledger is worth the same.

column1: Write sensitivity in rate form.
column2: \(S = -174 + 10\log_{10}R_b + (E_b/N_0)_{req} + \text{NF}\) dBm: halving the bit rate gains 3 dB at fixed modulation and code. Shannon's floor is \(E_b/N_0 \ge (2^\eta - 1)/\eta \to\) −1.59 dB.

column1: How are shadowing and fading margins sized?
column2: Lognormal shadowing: \(M = \sigma Q^{-1}(p_{out})\); Rayleigh fading: \(-10\log_{10}[-\ln(1 - p_{out})]\), about 20 dB for 1%. Combined (Suzuki), the margin is well below the sum.

column1: Edge versus area coverage?
column2: A margin for probability p at the cell edge gives higher coverage over the area, because most users are closer in (Jakes's formula): 75% at the edge is about 90% over the area at σ = 8 dB, n = 3.5.

column1: Why is cellular coverage uplink-limited?
column2: A 23 dBm handset through a small, hand-loaded antenna cannot match a base station's tens of watts and high-gain antennas, even though the base station has better noise figure and more receive antennas.

column1: Write the satellite link equation.
column2: \(C/N_0 = \text{EIRP} - L_{path} - L_{other} + G/T + 228.6\) dBHz, with slant range \(d = \sqrt{(R_E + h)^2 - R_E^2\cos^2\varepsilon} - R_E\sin\varepsilon\).

column1: How do NB-IoT, LoRa and Bluetooth Coded PHY reach long range?
column2: Narrow bandwidth, robust coding and repetition (\(10\log_{10}N\) per N repeats), about 20 dB beyond broadband budgets, paid in airtime and energy per message.

column1: How is an NR peak rate computed?
What sizes a modem's HARQ soft buffer?
column2: Each unfinished block's LLRs: up to 16 HARQ processes per cell (32 by capability), each storing information bits / \(R_{LBRM}\) (2/3) coded values at several bits each: megabytes per wide carrier.

column1: What sizes the layer-2 buffer?
column2: 3GPP's formula: the peak downlink plus uplink rates times the RLC round-trip time, for reordering and retransmission; wider subcarrier spacing shortens the round trip and the buffer.

column1: Compute a Wi-Fi PHY rate from its tone plan.
column2: \(R = N_{SD}\log_2M\,R_c/T_{sym}\) per stream, with \(T_{sym}\) = 12.8 µs plus a 0.8, 1.6 or 3.2 µs guard; 802.11be at 320 MHz has 3920 data subcarriers.

column1: Why does UWB use double-sided two-way ranging?
column2: Single-sided ranging's error is \((e_A - e_B)T_{reply}/2\), metres for ppm clocks; the double-sided formula cancels the reply times, leaving about the range times the mean clock offset.

column1: How does phase-based (channel-sounding) ranging work?
column2: The round-trip phase difference between tones Δf apart gives \(d = c\Delta\phi/(4\pi\Delta f)\), unambiguous to \(c/(2\Delta f)\); Bluetooth Channel Sounding measures tones on up to 72 channels at 1 MHz spacing.

column1: How do dual-frequency GNSS receivers remove ionospheric delay?
column2: The delay scales as \(1/f^2\), so the combination with weights \(f_1^2/(f_1^2 - f_2^2)\) and \(-f_2^2/(f_1^2 - f_2^2)\) cancels it, amplifying noise by about 2.6 for L1/L5 and 3.0 for L1/L2.

column1: What makes non-terrestrial NR hard?
column2: Doppler (about ±46 kHz at 2 GHz from a 600 km satellite, more than three 15 kHz subcarriers) and delay: low orbits fit within HARQ's process budget, but geostationary round trips need HARQ feedback disabled.
